messages.content: In this exchange, what does the reply mean? “Did you finish the poster?” “Not quite.”
It means the poster isn’t finished, but it doesn’t say exactly how much work remains.
Does it mean there’s only a little left?
It can suggest the work is close to finished, but it doesn’t tell us how much remains.
How is that different from “not yet”?
“Not yet” focuses on the fact that it isn’t finished at this time. “Not quite” more often suggests that it’s close, though neither gives an exact amount.
For “Did you finish the draft?” would “not yet” work if I don’t want to suggest how close I am?
Yes. “Not yet” says the draft isn’t finished without suggesting how close it is.
What’s the difference between “I packed the cups, plates and napkins.” and “I packed the cups, plates, and napkins.”?
The second version has a serial comma before “and.” In this simple list, it’s optional and doesn’t change the intended items.
Is one version wrong?
No. Both are acceptable; the choice often depends on the style you’re following.
Should I use the same style throughout a note?
Yes, consistency makes the punctuation easier to follow. If you’re using a particular style guide, follow its rule.
Using the serial comma, punctuate this: I brought pens pencils and paper.
I brought pens, pencils, and paper.
In this fictional message, what does the speaker think? “Thanks for checking. The blue cover looks good to me. I haven’t seen the green one.”
They think the blue cover looks good. They haven’t seen the green one, so the message doesn’t express an opinion about it.
Would “They prefer blue to green” be a fair paraphrase?
That overstates the message. They approve of blue, but they haven’t compared it with green.
Could they still end up preferring green?
Yes, they could. The message doesn’t tell us what they would think after seeing it.
Revise this comparison: “The blue cover is better than the green one, according to the speaker.”
“The speaker thinks the blue cover looks good but hasn’t seen the green one.”
What does “then” mean here? “The hall is ready.” “Then we can start.”
Here, “then” links being able to start to the hall being ready: given that it’s ready, we can start.
Does “then” always show a consequence?
No. It can also mark what happens next in a sequence.
Like “We ate, then left”?
Yes. There, “then” places leaving after eating; it doesn’t necessarily mean eating caused the departure.
I want to show a consequence in this line: “The files are ready. We can send them.” Can I add “then”?
Yes: “The files are ready. Then we can send them.” That links being able to send them to the files being ready.
